description: We are a passionate group of students who bring a diverse skill sets that include artificial intelligence and machine learning, physics, and research plus scientific outreach. We are going to work on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser this year.
summary: We have developed a software that engineers can use to facilitate mission planning for the moon based on map data, as we have integrated two Artificial Intelligence models to enhance this research process. We used a Classification Model to select the exact ideal landing location in the moon, this uses variables such as the communication availability, the proximity to water and other lunar resources, and the sunlight availability. The exact coordinates on the lunar surface are retrieved and sent to the Reinforcement Learning model which is then trained on the provided data using the simulation generating a CSV file, the CSV file can then be viewed on the main website to view the full flight path. The website contains information on past, current, and planned missions, providing data, photos, and information making it a valuable resource and learning tool for both learners, astrophysicists, and nasa engineers alike.

LunAI: A software for Lunar Space Mission Design with Integrated Orbital Mechanics and Surface Classification Technologies

Nicolas Dominguez Rodriguez, Adit Sood, Tanmay Devaraj, Arjun Bhatnagar, Ayaan Byahatti

 INTRODUCTION

Establishing a permanent human base on the Moon represents a fundamental milestone toward expanding humanity's reach as an interplanetary species by providing a strategic gateway for missions to Mars. This gateway enables essential spacecraft maintenance, allowing crews to leverage local lunar resources to repair and sustain vehicle components. Furthermore, it serves as a critical refueling station, extending mission lifespans and providing crucial operational redundancy. To maximize efficiency, reliability, and speed in establishing these settlements, automated mission planning models are essential. As mission complexity increases, advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) simulation tools—such as those powered by Reinforcement Learning (RL)—enable precise predictions of launch dynamics and flight paths while significantly reducing testing time and computational costs compared to manual methods. Integrating a surface classification model further allows for the reliable identification of optimal lunar landing sites. This enables the RL agent to optimize trajectory planning and fuel consumption for launch vehicles such as the Space Launch System (SLS), guaranteeing successful mission outcomes. The framework explored in this paper combines an SLS flight dynamics simulation with a lunar topography classification model to enhance overall mission design. By embedding these techniques into real-world orbital launch scenarios, this work provides an integrated suite of tools designed to advance safety, cost-effectiveness, and operational performance in lunar exploration.

METHODS AND EXPERIMENTATION

Artificial Intelligence Subsystems

Machine Learning Training Methods

AI systems are primarily trained using three fundamental paradigms: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning handles regression and classification tasks using labeled datasets (consisting of independent predictor variables or features to predict dependent labels), whereas unsupervised learning analyzes unlabeled data to uncover underlying structural patterns. Reinforcement learning trains agents within interactive environments designed to emulate dynamic, real-world operational challenges.

The LunAI system integrates two key machine learning subsystems: a surface classification model to evaluate potential landing sites and a reinforcement learning model to optimize trajectory planning and fuel consumption. Figure 1 illustrates the overarching system architecture.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 1: High-level architectural flowchart of the LunAI system detailing the data flow from lunar surface classification to reinforcement learning trajectory optimization.

The first subsystem of LunAI is a lunar landing site classification model designed to identify suitable landing locations. The model utilizes high-resolution topographical datasets acquired by NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) for three target regions near the lunar south pole: Connecting Ridge (Site 1), Shackleton Rim (Site 4), and Malapert Massif (Site 23).

These datasets, stored as GeoTIFF (TIF) rasters, provide precise measurements of elevation, slope angles, and associated uncertainty metrics. The processing pipeline analyzes localized terrain variations across each region to locate areas characterized by gentle slopes, low roughness, and sufficient spatial extent for safe spacecraft landing. A supervised Random Forest classifier evaluates these spatial features to rank candidate landing sites. The top ten sites per region are indexed by latitude and longitude coordinates, and multi-panel heatmaps are generated to visualize slope distributions and candidate site suitability.

The second subsystem is an orbital mechanics and trajectory optimization simulator integrated with Reinforcement Learning (RL). A custom simulation environment models the flight profile of the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket from initial launch conditions to target lunar coordinates. Incorporating rocket mass, velocity, thrust dynamics, atmospheric drag, and gravitational accelerations, the simulator calculates the continuous physics governing spacecraft motion over time.

A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent, implemented using TensorFlow, interacts with the environment to optimize flight paths. By controlling thrust magnitude and vectoring, the agent learns to balance fuel consumption against targeting accuracy based on a structured reward function. Through iterative training episodes, the PPO model converges toward trajectory profiles that minimize propellant expenditure while maintaining high guidance accuracy.

Data Collection and Processing

Data Sources for the Classification Model

Topographic data were obtained from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), using the LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites resource. Three candidate landing regions were selected - Connecting Ridge (Site 1), Shackleton Rim (Site 4) and Malapert Massif (Site 23). Each site is distributed as GeoTIFF (TIF) rasters at a resolution of 5 m per pixel. Sites 1 and 4 cover 16 km × 16 km (3200 × 3200 pixels), and Site 23 covers 21 km × 21 km (4200 × 4200 pixels).

Five raster layers are read for each site - surface elevation, slope, slope uncertainty, vertical error, and a LOLA shot-density (point count) layer.

Three further datasets, at 60 m per pixel and covering 85°S to 90°S, supply the non-topographic criteria. These come from NASA Goddard's Planetary Geodesy Data Archive: the average Earth-visibility fraction, the average solar-illumination fraction, and a permanently shadowed region (PSR) mask. These layers are not inputs to the classifier.

Raster Processing and Georeferencing

GeoTIFFs were read with the tifffile library and cast to 32-bit floating-point arrays, with numpy and scipy.ndimage used for all array operations. Georeferencing was taken directly from the GeoTIFF ModelPixelScale and ModelTiepoint tags. All data use a South Polar Stereographic projection on a sphere of radius 1,737.4 km, with a standard parallel at 90°S and a central meridian of 0°. Pixel coordinates were converted to latitude and longitude using an inverse polar stereographic projection implemented from Snyder's formulas. A forward-then-inverse round-trip test recovered the original coordinates exactly.

The topography and illumination files use the same sphere and projection parameters, so they are numerically compatible; this compatibility is assumed rather than verified in code.

Pixels with a missing slope or elevation value are flagged invalid. To stop a single bad pixel from corrupting its neighbourhood statistics, missing values are temporarily filled before filtering and restored to missing afterwards. Any pixel that is invalid in any feature is excluded from training and prediction. No missing values were found in the rasters used.

Feature Engineering

A terrain feature vector is computed for every pixel using a sliding window of 21 × 21 pixels (105 m). The window is centred on each pixel, so neighbouring windows overlap and the terrain is not divided into separate tiles. Ten features are derived from the five rasters:

Together, these ten features characterize local steepness, surface roughness, topographic relief, and measurement accuracy. Because tree-based models are invariant to monotonic transformations, no feature scaling was required prior to model training.

Training Dataset and Labels

Each training sample consists of a ten-dimensional feature vector for an individual pixel. Pixels located inside pre-defined region-of-interest (ROI) polygons are labeled 1 (candidate landing zone), while remaining pixels are labeled 0. The ROI polygons were retrieved from original NASA archive shapefiles (Site01_ROIs and Site04_ROIs) and rasterized into binary masks. Site 23 lacks ROI shapefile labels and is used exclusively for inference.

To mitigate extreme class imbalance, negative samples were drawn at an 8:1 ratio relative to positive samples for training, and class-weighted tree balancing was applied. Negative sampling was restricted to pixels positioned at least 6 pixels (30 m) away from ROI polygon boundaries to prevent ambiguous label assignments. For validation, a 50:1 negative-to-positive ratio was used to reflect operational terrain distribution.

Classification Model Architecture

Choice of Algorithm

A Random Forest classifier was selected for its capacity to evaluate multi-dimensional terrain features concurrently, capture complex non-linear feature interactions (such as slope tolerances relative to surface roughness), and prevent overfitting through decision tree ensembling. Additionally, tree ensembles provide intrinsic feature importance metrics, improving model interpretability.

Implementation

The forest was implemented as a custom class, RandomForestLite, wrapping 400 independent scikit-learn DecisionTreeClassifier objects. The standard sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier could not be imported on the development machine because of a system security policy, so bootstrap resampling and per-split feature subsampling were implemented manually. The method is algorithmically equivalent to a standard Random Forest.

Bootstrap Sampling: For each decision tree, a bootstrap sample with replacement is generated from the pooled training dataset, ensuring sample variance across the ensemble.

Feature Subsampling: At each split node, approximately three features (sqrt of 10) are randomly sampled. This decorrelates individual trees and prevents dominant terrain metrics (such as raw slope) from biasing the entire forest structure.

Ensemble Prediction: Class-1 probability outputs across all 400 trees are aggregated via soft voting to produce a continuous terrain suitability score between 0 and 1 for every pixel.

Regularization: Overfitting is controlled by capping tree depth at 12, specifying a minimum leaf size of 5 samples, and leveraging bootstrap aggregation.

The deployed model was trained on Site 1 and Site 4 combined and then applied to all three sites.

Landing Suitability Scoring

The Random Forest evaluates terrain only. Two other criteria are measured directly from NASA datasets, with no machine learning involved.

Communication suitability. The Earth-visibility raster gives the fraction of an 18.6-year lunar nutation cycle during which Earth is above the local horizon. This value was calculated by the data provider using horizon ray-tracing. The 60 m raster is resampled onto the 5 m site grid by bilinear interpolation, and the stored scale factor (4 × 10⁻⁵) is applied to convert raw integers to a 0 to 1 fraction.

Water-ice proximity. The PSR mask is an effectively binary layer of permanently shadowed ground. A Euclidean distance transform gives each location's straight-line distance in kilometres to the nearest shadowed pixel. This measures proximity to cold traps, where ice is thermally stable. It does not detect ice.

Solar illumination. The average solar-illumination fraction is computed and reported for every candidate, but it is not part of the weighted score.

The composite score for a candidate region is:

Score = 0.60 * P_terrain + 0.30 * V_Earth + 0.10 * W

where W = 1 − min(d, 50) / 50, and d is the distance in km to the nearest permanently shadowed pixel.

Terrain probability and Earth visibility are already on a 0 to 1 scale, so only the water distance is rescaled. The 50 km cap and the 60/30/10 weights are design choices, not values fitted to outcome data; they place the highest priority on safe terrain, then on communication, then on resource access.

Site Ranking and Visualisation

Pixels with a terrain probability of at least 0.80 are marked as safe. Contiguous safe pixels are grouped into candidate regions using connected-component labelling, and regions smaller than 150 pixels (3,750 m²) are discarded. Each remaining region receives a composite score, where the terrain, Earth-visibility and illumination values are the means over the whole region. The ten regions with the highest composite scores are reported. The representative coordinate of each region is its single pixel of highest terrain probability, converted to latitude and longitude by the inverse stereographic projection.

For each site, a heat map with a 2 × 3 grid of panels is produced: raw slope, terrain suitability probability, solar illumination, Earth visibility, water distance, and the composite score. The ten ranked positions are overlaid as numbered markers, along with nearby named features. A CSV of the ten candidates (rank, score, component values, area and coordinates) is also exported.

[Figure 3: Six-panel heat map with the ten ranked candidates highlighted]

No minimum spacing is enforced between candidates, so the top-ranked regions can cluster; at Site 23, ranks 1 to 3 fall within about 1 km of each other.

Model Evaluation

Because the positive samples come from a small number of spatially contiguous polygons, a random split of pixels would place neighbouring, highly correlated pixels in both training and test sets and inflate performance. The model was therefore validated with a leave-one-site-out scheme: it was trained on one site and tested on the other, with the test labels coming from a geographically separate region.

Orbital Simulator for the Reinforcement Learning Model

Due to the lack of open-source flight telemetry data for the Space Launch System (SLS), Falcon 9 telemetry data was utilized to verify the validity and accuracy of our orbital simulator. The Falcon 9 flight telemetry data used to compare the performance of the agent’s actions in the simulator was taken from publicly available sources in JavaScript Object Notation - JSON - format. The dataset, a sample is shown in Figure 1, includes variables like time, velocity, acceleration, downrange distance, altitude, angle and dynamic pressure (q).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Tabular dataset snippet of Falcon 9 telemetry recording time, velocity, altitude, acceleration, downrange distance, angle, and dynamic pressure." ]

Figure 1: Sample dataset of Falcon 9 flight telemetry data (Credit: GitHub)

Mass Flow Rate Derivation

As seen in Figure 1, the data provided publicly does not contain information on the mass flow rate over time, nor the fuel left, which is necessary to compare the performance of the agent with the actual flight to correctly evaluate if it has achieved efficient fuel consumption in the mission.

Therefore, the variable ṁ, representing mass flow rate,  would be estimated every second with the information provided from the dataset by combining two main equations that link thrust and resultant force to derive acceleration and, in turn, the mass flow rate.

The force equation is dependent on the current mass of the rocket multiplied by its corresponding acceleration at a time. This can be translated into the following equation:

F=mtat→F=(mt-ṁt)*at

The thrust equation is dependent on the current mass flow rate and the exhaust velocity (ve) the pressure of the exhaust (pe) and the environmental pressure (p0) and the area of the exhaust (Ae). This is communicated in the equation below:

F= ṁt *ve+(pe-p0)*Ae

For the simplification of this model, the variables ve, pe and Ae are modelled to be constant however for more realistic scenarios the environmental pressure is automatically updated every second as the rocket’s trajectory increases altitude (h) – shown by the formula:

p0=101325e^-(h/8.434)

By combining the equations above, the final formula to calculate ṁ is derived:

ṁt=atmt-(pe-p0)*Ae/(ve+ at)

Preliminary Data Analysis

Mass Distribution

The Falcon 9 rocket consists of a two-stage rocket, where the first stage contains a total of 432,800 kilograms (kg) and the second stage contains a total mass of 119,500 kg; the total dry mass of the rocket is around 32,300 kg. These mass values are crucial for the previously derived mass flow rate equation as, depending on the stage it is in, the mass will vary from around 432,800 kg in stage 1 to 119,500 kg in stage 2, which would greatly affect the output.

Velocity and Acceleration Analysis

The velocity seems to split into two crescent curves, shown in Figure 2, with the second curve having a much steeper gradient. Another important detail to mention is that at the point of separation, there is a small dent, happening at about 145 seconds (s), which can be interpreted as the stage separation when the rocket turns off its stage 1 engines – this event is known as the main engine cut-off (MECO). Around 10 seconds after this happens, at 155s, the second engine start (SES) occurs; this effectively separates the first and second stages of flight and is the cause of the build-up of speed at 155s. Towards the end of the flight, at 565s in, acceleration suddenly halts, representing the second engine cut-off (SECO).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Plots of Falcon 9 velocity and altitude over time with key mission events (MECO, SES, SECO) marked by vertical dashed lines." ]

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Plots showing acceleration and dynamic pressure vs time for Falcon 9, depicting peak dynamic pressure (Max-Q) and engine cut-off events." ]

Figure 2.1: Velocity over time for Falcon 9

Figure 2.2: Acceleration over time for Falcon 9

These events have a noticeable effect on the velocity (Figure 2.1) but are most evident in the acceleration over time of the rocket (Figure 2.2). As can be seen in Figures 2.1 and 2.2, the acceleration presents sudden falls as these events occur, which in turn affect the dynamics of the velocity over time. This property of the dependence of the velocity on the acceleration is crucial for the building of the environment.

Modelled Mass Flow Rate

With reference to Figure 4, it is evident that the Falcon 9 rocket has a mass flow rate of approximately 2700 kgs-1 for the first stage.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Line graphs showing propellant remaining and modeled mass flow rate over time for Stage 1 and Stage 2 of Falcon 9." ]

Figure 4: Mass flow rate (kgs-1) over time for the Falcon 9

The value stated above is confirmed by finding the mass flow rate values of known variables in the thrust equation below:

FT= m×vem=FTve

In the above equation, the exhaust velocity is equivalent to the product of the specific impulse and the gravitational acceleration in metres per second squared (ms-2); the specific impulse of a Merlin is around 282 s, meaning the value of the exhaust velocity in the equation is 2766.42 ms-1. The thrust of an individual Merlin sea-level engine - for the first stage - is around 845 kN, which, when divided by the exhaust velocity, gives a final mass flow rate of 305.45 kgs-1. As previously stated, the total mass flow rate for the first stage is around 2700 kgs-1, which, when divided by the number of engines (nine engines) in the first stage, gives an average of 300 kgs-1, meaning that it is only off by 5.45 kgs-1.

From Figure 4, it can be seen that the second stage has an average mass flow rate of 285 kgs-1 for the second stage. The specific impulse of the Merlin vacuum engine is 348 s, meaning that the exhaust velocity is around 3413.88 ms-1, the thrust of the second stage is 981 kN, which, when divided by the exhaust velocity, gives an estimated 287.36 kgs-1, which is greater than the actual value by only 2.36 kgs-1 which shows the calculation to be quite accurate.

Another detail to point out is the clear indentation shown in the mass flow rate of the first stage as consumption gradually reduces at around 70 s, which caused an increase in power. This pattern can be represented by a graph of dynamic pressure over time, such as the one shown in Figure 5.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Line graph of Falcon 9 dynamic pressure over time, highlighting the throttle-down effect near Max-Q around 70 seconds." ]

Figure 5: Dynamic pressure over time for the Falcon 9 rocket.

The dynamic pressure of a spacecraft is the structural stress the rocket accumulates over time due to air resistance. In this scenario, the Falcon 9 reached a maximum dynamic pressure at 70 seconds and it is precisely when the mass flow rate noticeably decreases to prevent really high acceleration from irreparably damaging the spacecraft.

Fuel Remaining over Time

The remaining fuel is modelled over time using the following equation:

mt=mt-1-mt

Where mt is the total mass of the Falcon 9 rocket, and in this scenario it is necessary to subtract the dry mass at each stage from the total mass. For the first stage, this would be around 32,300 kg; for the second stage, it is around 9,500 kg. The result of the model is depicted in Figure 6.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Graph illustrating remaining propellant mass depleting across Stage 1 and Stage 2 throughout the flight duration." ]

Figure 6: Propellant (kg) over time for the Falcon 9 rocket.

Since the mass flow rate of the first stage was around nine times greater than that of the second stage, the amount of fuel depleted during the first stage was much greater than for the second. It depleted around 400,000 kg of fuel in 145 s, however, it is important to note that for the stage separation, specifically at MECO, the fuel remaining is not exactly the amount of fuel left for only the second stage - around 110,000 which was actually 147,200 kg.

The velocity the first stage of the Falcon 9 needs to achieve to successfully operate an ASDS landing - landing on a drone ship - is around 700 ms-1. Additionally, the mass at the stage of separation is around 22,800 kg – with only dry mass considered – for the first stage, which can be used to determine the amount of fuel necessary using the following formula:

∆v=veln m0+mfm0 → mf=m0e∆vve-1

In this case, mf would be the resulting propellant mass needed to perform a landing in a drone pad in the ocean, m0 is the initial mass at stage separation, ve is the exhaust velocity, which is around 2700 ms-1, and ∆v would be the velocity required for the successful landing added to the previous velocity achieved - which is 1665 ms-1.

This results in an estimate of around 31,000 kg of fuel required for a successful ASDS landing. To work out the amount of fuel modelled, the amount of fuel for the second stage (110,000 kg) is taken away from the current amount of fuel at MECO (147,000 kg) which results in around 37,000 kg, which is only a 6,000 kg difference from the data observed, however, this additional fuel is within a 20% margin, which allows for redundancy and safety of the flight. Most importantly, this calculation confirms the accuracy of the modelled mass flow rate and fuel progression over time as it adjusted the fuel mass to the realistic flight scenario.

Towards the end of the flight, at SECO, a similar pattern is seen: the second stage ends with around 1,640 kg of fuel, which is probably needed for redundancy or additional maneuvers of the flight. This is a huge milestone for the experiment as it confirms that the model successfully prevented negative values of fuel consumed over time and properly mimics realistic flight scenarios.

Interestingly, the actual flight being analysed (the Orbcomm OG2 flight 25) performed an ASDS landing, meaning that the proof of accuracy of the model has been successful and it could be used to correctly predict a flight event using it.

Simulator Design

Deriving Acceleration

In order to properly run the simulator, it is necessary to derive the acceleration of the Falcon 9 every second, which only depends on the mass flow rate.

Three main forces are interacting and affecting the rocket in the simulator: thrust (the propelling force that launches it the opposite direction to where the combustion is occurring and is exiting the exhaust), air resistance (under atmospheric conditions, the air resistance is the opposing force to any direction the rocket is facing, so to calculate the resultant force between the first two mentioned, we must subtract this from thrust) and gravity (influential to the model as it is magnitude derived from the rocket’s angle at an instant).

Thrust Equations

Similarly, the simplified formula for thrust involves mainly the mass flow rate, which is controlled by the agent, and the exhaust velocity, which is maintained as a constant for simplifying the model.

FT= mve

However, as we are considering atmospheric conditions to maximize realism of the simulation, it is important to add the pressure difference between the exhaust and the environment at a certain altitude; therefore, the complete formula for the thrust is the following:

F=mve+(pe-p0)Ae

The only two variables that are prone to change every time step are the mass flow rate and the thrust at each instant. The rest of the variables are constant or have changed at different times: 

  • Exhaust velocity is set at 2570 ms-1 and for the second stage it is 3350 ms-1
  • The pressure in the exhaust is 70,927.5 Pa; however, for the second stage it is 0 Pa (since the rocket is outside the atmosphere)
  • Environmental pressure is dependent on the altitude achieved as it follows the exponential function: p0=101325e-h8.434 where the altitude is processed every time step of the flight and the pressure at sea level is 101,325 Pa – this value is automatically set to zero by the function itself or an if statement built-in the programme.
  • The area of the exhaust is the total sum of the individual 

Air Resistance Equations

To accurately simulate realistic atmospheric conditions, it is essential to incorporate the effects of dynamic pressure, which plays a critical role in determining the aerodynamic forces acting on a rocket during flight. Dynamic pressure is computed using the following relationship:

q=1/2*v^2

Both density and air resistance are time-dependent and vary throughout the rocket’s ascent. Specifically, air density is influenced by altitude and follows a relationship similar to the one used in calculating environmental pressure. At sea level, air density is around 1.225 kgm-3, and it decreases with increasing altitude. 

To comprehensively model the aerodynamic drag acting on the vehicle, the drag force FD is determined using the standard drag equation:

Fd=1/2*v^2*Cd*A

Two variables are added in the formula to fully model air resistance:

  • Cd is the drag coefficient, which, for the purposes of this simulation, is assumed to be a constant value of 0.4 to balance computational simplicity with physical accuracy.
  • A represents the reference area of the vehicle exposed to the airflow. For the Falcon 9, this is approximated as a constant value of 10.5 m2.

This approach allows for a reasonably accurate yet computationally efficient modeling of air resistance, which is a key force acting against the rocket's ascent through the atmosphere. The final formula derived is as follows:

Fd=Cd*A*v^2/2

Gravity Equations

The most influential factor of a rocket’s flight is the gravitational force acting upon it, which is modelled by the standard weight equation:

Fg=mt*gt

Where as clarified before, the variable mass in this scenario is constantly changed every time step depending on the mass flow rate, however, to adjust for realistic scenarios, the gravity is not kept as a constant, but rather as a variable that is affected by the increasing altitudes achieved as well:

gt=mg/(6378000+ht)^2

Where m and g are constants referring to the mass of the Earth (5.972×1024 kg) gravitational constant (6.67×1011 Nm2kg-2) and the value in the denominator (6,378,000) represents the radius of the Earth in metres.

However, the direction of the rocket will affect the magnitude of the derived value of gt, which is modified as the following formula depending on the instant angle at each time step:

gt=gtsin theta

By combining both above formulae, the final formula used for the resultant force can be achieved:

Fg=mtgtsin theta

Resultant Forces

After deriving the formulae for the three principal forces acting on the rocket, it is necessary to calculate the resultant force which is simply subtracting the weight and the drag of the rocket from its current thrust which is also equivalent to the mass at each time step multiplied by its acceleration.

Fnet=mtat=Ft-(Fd+Fg)

To work out acceleration at an instant we divide the net force calculated by the mass at each instant - where the mass at each instant is the current mass flow rate subtracted from the last recorded mass of each time step.

at=Fnet/(mt-1-mt)

Kinematics

By rearranging the traditional formula for acceleration, we can work out the new speed of every time step. 

vt=vt-1+at*∆t

Therefore the only additional step for the new speed is just the addition of the previous velocity  with the acceleration multiplied by the time step, which in this case is one second.

Furthermore, to work out the flight profile of the Falcon 9 flight in the simulator, it is necessary to work out the distance travelled every time step both in downrange distance and altitude

The following velocity formula is used and rearranged to find the distance travelled over time:

Vertical:

yt=yt-1+vt * sin theta*∆t

Horizontal:

xt=xt-1+vtcos theta*∆t

Simulator Results

The simulator was tested with the previously modeled mass flow rate values from section 2.7.1, and the results of the telemetry are validated with the score given by the r2 formula, where the squared difference between the actual and simulated value is calculated and the accuracy is given as a percentage, the results are the following:

Figures 7 to 10 show both the modelled flight scenario, represented by a blue line, and the actual flight scenario, which is represented by the red line in the graphs.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Overlay comparison plot of simulated vs actual Falcon 9 velocity profiles showing close alignment over time." ]

Figure 7: Simulation of velocity over time for the Falcon 9

As shown in Figure 7, the velocity for both the simulated and the actual scenario are very close with no large discrepancies close. in the beginning and middle of the flight, the simulated version did not calculate a velocity as high as the actual velocity, however, towards the end, the modelled velocity is slightly higher than the actual velocity, the actual final velocity being 7219 ms-1, while the simulated one is 7247 ms-1, meaning that it is only over by 28 ms-1.

Even if it seems a large amount, the r2 score of the velocity is 99.91%.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Comparison plot of simulated acceleration against actual telemetry data over time, illustrating minor model offsets during stage transitions." ]

It is evident that in this scenario, the acceleration’s predictive values output by the simulator are much lower than the actual values for most of the flight; this has occurred since the only thrust sources considered were the main merlin engines propelling the rocket upwards, and in stages like MECO or SECO, there may have been other thrusters helping prevent the deceleration presented in the blue curve, however, towards the end, the simulated rocket has picked up a slightly greater acceleration than the actual flight, which in turn may have increased the final simulated velocity to the amount mentioned in the previous section.

To build a completely integrated system that can fully plan missions where the moon is the final destination, we need to build an orbital mechanics simulator that can accurately model the trajectory of the moon over the same period. 

Deriving Acceleration on the Moon

Just like referred back in section 2.9.1, to derive the acceleration of any object, firstly the resultant forces must be worked out. In this scenario, the forces acting will be measured in each axis separately, because this way, the data obtained can be directly compared with the data saved in JPL’s database.

Lunar Orbital Data Analysis

Between the moon and the Earth, the only force influencing the dynamics of the object is the centripetal force, which is the gravitational attraction between the earth and the moon. This force is modelled with the following formula:

Gf=gMm/r^2

Where g is the gravitational constant (6.67 × 10-11 m3 kg-1 s-2), M is the mass of Earth (5.9722 × 1024 kg), and m would be the mass of the moon (7.3477 × 1022 kg). However, this force, only gives us the magnitude of the gravitational force, the force distribution is shown in the graph below:

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Diagram showing vector decomposition of gravitational centripetal forces acting on the Moon along Cartesian axes." ]

Figure 13: Distribution of gravitational forces on the moon

To calculate each force independently, the overall force needs to be multiplied by the ratio between the difference between the corresponding coordinates of the moon and the center of the earth, this is worked out with the following general formula:

Gf(x,y,z)=gMmΔ(x,y,z)/r^3

After using this universal function for the lunar orbital mechanics simulation, the starting conditions of the moon’s velocity in each axis, and the moon’s starting position in the coordinate system is the same one as JPL’s recorded dataset that we obtained, to then compare both results and check for accuracy. 

This formula to derive the force is then used to work out the acceleration, velocity, and displacement of the moon’s orbit throughout its trajectory by using the same logic described in section 2.9.5 and 2.9.6, as the resultant force is divided by the mass of the moon to work out the new acceleration, and this acceleration will be used to update the velocity, which in turns updates the displacement in each axis individually. The simulator ran only 31 iterations, which matches the amount of records stored in the Horizon Results database, which we would use to compare it with, for this reason, the time step is set to 24 * 60 * 60, which is 86400 seconds, as this is the amount of seconds in a day. Reinforcement Learning Landing Model

Role of the Model

The second subsystem of LunAI plans how a lander travels from low Earth orbit to a specified point on the Moon's surface, such as one of the sites ranked by the classifier in Part 1. The objective is to reach the target coordinates with a soft touchdown (below 3 m/s) while using as little propellant as possible. The mission is split into two phases that use different methods:

Phase

Task

Method

Start

End

1

Trans-lunar injection

Lambert's problem (classical orbital mechanics, no learning)

Circular orbit at about 300 km

Arrival near the target

2

Final descent and landing

Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) agent

About 15 km above the target

Touchdown

A first design asked a single PPO agent to fly the whole mission from the launch pad. It never reached the Moon , so the transfer to the Moon was handed to classical orbital mechanics and reinforcement learning was kept for the part where it works, the final descent. Public flight data for the Space Launch System (SLS) does not exist, so the simulator's shared physics is validated against Falcon 9 telemetry instead .

Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO)

PPO is a reinforcement learning algorithm that trains a small neural network (two hidden layers of 64 units) to act as the lander's controller. The agent flies many simulated descents and is scored by the reward function (Section 3), and the network is adjusted so that actions that earned more reward become more likely. PPO clips each update (clip range 0.2) so the new behaviour stays close to the old one, which stops a single bad update from ruining a controller that was working.

Why PPO

PPO was chosen because it suits the landing problem. The lander is controlled by its throttle and thrust direction, which are continuous values, and PPO can output them directly. Learning also has to be stable. In a sensitive physical simulation, a single bad update can turn a controller that lands into one that crashes, and PPO's clipped updates prevent this by keeping each new policy close to the previous one. Additionally, there are no known optimal landings to copy, so the agent must learn from the reward alone, and PPO does this by trial and error in the simulator.

Usage

PPO controls only the final descent (Phase 2), starting about 15 km above the target. Phase 1 uses Lambert's problem. At each step the agent reads the 24-number observation and returns the throttle, and the thrust direction in the full-control version. The best-working version learned only the throttle .

Environment State and Action Space

The environment state represents the information provided to the AI agent to understand the current conditions of the spacecraft during the simulation. In LUNAI, the observation consists of 24 different values, which provide information about the spacecraft's position, velocity, orientation and propulsion conditions.

The observation includes the following:

  • Rocket position: The three-dimensional position of the spacecraft relative to Earth.
  • Rocket velocity: The spacecraft's velocity along the three spatial axes.
  • Attitude: The current orientation of the spacecraft.
  • Moon-relative position and velocity: The spacecraft's position and velocity in relation to the Moon.
  • Target-relative position: The distance and direction between the spacecraft and the specified lunar landing location.
  • Mass fraction: The remaining spacecraft mass relative to its initial mass.
  • Stage propellant fractions: The remaining fuel in each propulsion stage.
  • Stage index: The currently active propulsion stage.
  • Elapsed time: The proportion of the total permitted simulation time that has passed.

These values are normalised using predefined constants before being supplied to the neural network, allowing the agent to process the different observations consistently.

During every step of the simulation, the environment updates the spacecraft's position, velocity, mass and other physical conditions based on the forces acting upon it. It then generates a new observation for the agent. The environment also performs termination checks to determine whether the simulation should continue or end. These checks include:

  • If the spacecraft impacts the Earth, the episode terminates.
  • If the spacecraft reaches the lunar surface, the episode terminates and its landing accuracy and velocity are evaluated.
  • If the spacecraft escapes the simulated Earth–Moon system, the episode terminates.
  • If the simulation exceeds its permitted duration without achieving a landing, the episode terminates.

The action space of the environment allows the agent to influence the spacecraft and modify its state at every time step. Unlike the previous experiment, which used a discrete action space with only two possible outputs, LUNAI uses a continuous action space. The agent can control two main aspects of the spacecraft's movement: the magnitude of its thrust through throttle adjustments and the direction in which the thrust is applied through three-dimensional directional controls.

This allows the agent to make more flexible adjustments to the spacecraft's movement rather than choosing between a limited number of predefined actions. The environment automatically normalises the directional inputs before applying them to the simulated spacecraft.

However, the extent of the agent's control depends on the configuration being used. In the partially trained PPO configuration, the agent learns to regulate the throttle while a scripted controller automatically adjusts the thrust direction to oppose the spacecraft's velocity. A separate fully scripted configuration was also tested, while the fully autonomous PPO configuration, in which the agent controls both throttle and direction, has not yet been consistently validated.

Reward Function

As all reinforcement learning models, deep within its policy it is naturally to maximize the The reward has four parts, which together balance closeness to the target, a gentle arrival and fuel use:

  1. Progress shaping. The agent is rewarded only when it gets closer to the target than ever before in the episode. Rewarding the raw change in distance each step would let it collect reward by moving back and forth.
  2. Speed penalty near the Moon. A penalty proportional to the speed relative to the Moon, active only within a set distance of the Moon, pushes the agent to brake on approach.
  3. Fuel penalty on landing. A penalty proportional to the propellant used, applied only if the episode ends in an actual landing.
  4. Terminal rewards and penalties. Ground impact on Earth gives −100. A lunar impact gives a reward based on accuracy and impact speed. Escaping the Earth–Moon system gives −50, and timing out without landing gives −50.

With d_t the distance to the target, d_best the smallest distance so far and v_M the speed relative to the Moon:

The balance between fuel and accuracy comes from how these terms combine. Because the fuel penalty applies only at landing, the agent is not discouraged from burning propellant early. It pays for fuel only if it lands, while the progress, speed and accuracy terms push it toward a precise, gentle touchdown. The timeout penalty was added after the agent found a loophole: it could avoid approaching the Moon at all to escape the speed penalty, so not landing had to cost something.

The network was optimised with the Adam optimiser, the Stable-Baselines3 default. Only the rollout length, batch size, learning rate and entropy coefficient were set explicitly. The other values are library defaults and were not tuned.

Training Cycle

The training loop consists of the following steps:

  1. The agent observes the current state through the 24-number observation.
  2. The agent samples an action (throttle and thrust direction) from its Gaussian policy. The sampling provides exploration, and the entropy bonus keeps the policy from becoming too narrow too early.
  3. The simulator advances one RK4 step and returns the next state and the reward.
  4. The transition is stored. Steps 1 to 4 repeat for 2,048 steps, and an episode that ends is reset. A descent episode lasts about 100 to 700 steps, so one batch holds roughly 3 to 20 episodes.
  5. The critic estimates the value V(s) of every step, and generalised advantage estimation turns these into an advantage for each action.
  6. The actor and critic are updated on the clipped objective in mini-batches of 256 for 10 epochs. With a single environment this is 8 mini-batches × 10 epochs = 80 gradient steps. 
  7. The batch is discarded, because it came from the old policy, and the next one is collected with the updated policy.

Computational Time Costs

The descent runs were trained on CPU. The long end-to-end runs covered tens of millions of timesteps and repeatedly ran out of memory, so they had to be resumed from saved checkpoints.

EVALUATION AND CONCLUSION

Limitations

Despite demonstrating the feasibility of combining classical orbital mechanics with reinforcement learning for lunar mission planning, the LUNAI project has several limitations that affect the accuracy, reliability and overall performance of the system. The three main limitations identified during development were:

  1. Simplified orbital mechanics and trajectory modelling: The first phase of the mission uses Lambert's problem to calculate a trans-lunar trajectory. However, this calculation relies on a patched-conic, two-body approximation in which the Lambert solution considers Earth's gravitational influence rather than accounting for the complete gravitational environment. Although the resulting trajectory is subsequently propagated through a more comprehensive simulator incorporating lunar gravity, this difference contributes to a remaining discrepancy between the calculated trajectory and the actual lunar target. The resulting closest approaches were approximately 271–579 km from the specified target coordinates.
  2. Challenges in reinforcement learning and policy optimisation: The initial approach attempted to train a single PPO agent to control the entire mission, from launch to lunar landing. However, the complexity of this task created significant training difficulties. The agent consistently failed to learn a successful Earth-to-Moon trajectory, even after tens of millions of training steps. Issues including unstable policy exploration, increasing action variability and computational memory limitations prevented the development of a reliable end-to-end control policy. Consequently, the project was redesigned to separate the trans-lunar journey from the final descent.
  3. Limited autonomy in the final landing phase: Although the redesigned system successfully demonstrated lunar descent, its most reliable landing results relied on scripted control mechanisms. The fully scripted approach achieved a soft landing at 2.22 m/s, while a partially trained PPO agent, which learned throttle control while using scripted directional control, achieved a landing velocity of 0.19 m/s. However, the fully autonomous PPO configuration, in which the agent controlled both thrust magnitude and direction, was not successfully validated as a consistently reliable landing method. Therefore, the current results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning for lunar descent, but do not yet establish the reliability of a completely autonomous landing system.

Future Growth

To improve the accuracy, autonomy and adaptability of the LUNAI system, future development should focus on the following areas:

  1. Developing a fully autonomous PPO agent: The primary objective is to improve the current reinforcement learning architecture so that the agent can independently control both thrust magnitude and direction during lunar descent. This would reduce dependence on predefined control rules and allow the system to learn more complex landing strategies through interaction with the simulation environment.
  2. Improving reward function and policy optimisation: Further refinement of the reward function could improve the balance between landing accuracy, final velocity and fuel consumption. The objective would be to ensure that the agent consistently prioritises a safe and accurate touchdown while minimising unnecessary fuel expenditure.
  3. Increasing the accuracy of the orbital mechanics simulator: The simulator could be further developed to incorporate more comprehensive gravitational modelling, additional celestial-body interactions and more accurate trajectory propagation. This would help reduce the discrepancies between the approximated Lambert trajectory and the full numerical simulation.
  4. Expanding physical modelling and vehicle adaptability: Future versions could incorporate more detailed propulsion models, variable engine characteristics and additional environmental effects. The simulator could also be adapted to represent different launch vehicles and spacecraft configurations, allowing the framework to be applied to a wider range of spaceflight scenarios.

Conclusion and Impact

The LUNAI project demonstrates a hybrid approach to lunar mission planning by combining classical orbital mechanics with reinforcement learning. Rather than relying entirely on an AI agent to learn the complete mission through trial and error, the final architecture separates the journey into two independently managed phases. The first phase employs Lambert's orbital mechanics to calculate the trans-lunar transfer, while the second uses a PPO-based reinforcement learning environment to investigate autonomous lunar descent and landing.

The initial attempt to train a single PPO agent to manage the entire mission proved unsuccessful, highlighting the challenges associated with learning complex, long-duration spacecraft trajectories from scratch. However, restructuring the problem into smaller components produced substantially more promising results. The Lambert-based trajectory calculations successfully brought the simulated spacecraft within approximately 271–579 km of the specified lunar target. Furthermore, the landing experiments demonstrated that a scripted control strategy could achieve a soft landing at 2.22 m/s, while a partially trained PPO configuration achieved a final landing velocity of 0.19 m/s.

Although the system has not yet demonstrated a consistently successful, fully autonomous Earth-to-Moon mission, the results establish a foundation for further investigation into the application of artificial intelligence in spaceflight trajectory optimization. In particular, the project illustrates how reinforcement learning can be applied to a complex control problem by isolating a more manageable phase of the mission, while classical mathematical methods handle the initial orbital transfer.

Ultimately, LUNAI explores the potential of integrating computational orbital mechanics and machine learning to support future space exploration. With further improvements to physical modelling, policy training and autonomous control, this framework could contribute to the development of more efficient and adaptable methods for spacecraft trajectory planning and lunar landing operations.
